chunks.content:
My final model is the 6-feature logistic regression with a cutoff of 0.60. On the validation set, which keeps the natural fraud rate, it caught 62 of the 74 fraudulent claims, with sensitivity 0.838, specificity 0.850, precision 0.646, F1 0.729 and AUC 0.855.

The tuned random forest overfitted. It scored 0.982 accuracy on the training data but did worse than the logistic regression on every validation metric (F1 0.659, AUC 0.825). Its cross-validated F1 of 0.926 was also too optimistic, because I oversampled before cross-validation and copies of the same fraud claims ended up in both training and test folds. The validation set was never resampled, so its numbers are the ones I trust.

Most of the signal comes from incident severity and the high-risk hobby flag. Incident severity and insured hobbies had the two biggest spreads in fraud rate in the EDA, and in the final model the hobby flag and the three severity levels have the four largest coefficients. Severity makes sense, since Major Damage claims were fraudulent 60.9% of the time. The hobby flag does not: there is no real reason chess and cross-fit players would have fraud rates of 90.6% and 76.0%, so I think it is an artefact of the synthetic data and would not carry over to real claims.

The 0.60 cutoff treats a missed fraud and a false alarm as equally costly, which is not true for an insurer. The next step would be to set the cutoff from the real cost of each type of error, and to move the oversampling inside each cross-validation fold.
chunks.contextBlurb: The excerpt reports the performance of the final 6‑feature logistic regression model and compares it to a tuned random forest, explaining why the logistic regression is preferred and discussing key predictors such as incident severity and a hobby flag, as well as future steps for cost‑based thresholding and proper cross‑validation.

chunks.content:
Classifying auto insurance claims as fraudulent or legitimate using logistic regression
and random forest, on 1,000 historical claims with a 24.7% fraud rate.

**On held-out claims, logistic regression catches 84% of frauds at 85% specificity
(F1 0.729, AUC 0.855). It beats a tuned random forest on every validation metric, even
though the forest scores 0.982 accuracy on the training set (1.000 before tuning).**

## The problem

An insurer reviewing motor claims has two ways to lose money. Paying a fraudulent claim
costs the payout. Investigating an honest one costs an adjuster's time and irritates a
customer who did nothing wrong. Reviewing every claim is not affordable, so the question
is which claims to look at.

The model's first job is therefore to rank claims by risk, so a small review team can
start at the top. Picking the cutoff on that ranking comes second.

## Data

1,000 claims, 40 columns, covering policy details, the insured party, the incident, and
claim amounts. Target is `fraud_reported` (Y/N), 24.7% positive.

| Step | Rows | Columns |
|---|---|---|
| Raw | 1,000 | 40 |
| After dropping `_c39` (entirely empty) | 1,000 | 39 |
| After dropping one invalid row | 999 | 39 |
| After dropping identifiers, adding derived features | 999 | 35 |
| Train / validation (70/30, stratified) | 699 / 300 | 34 |
chunks.contextBlurb: The excerpt describes the Fraudulent Claim Detection project, which uses logistic regression and random forest models to classify 1,000 auto insurance claims as fraudulent or legitimate, achieving an 84% fraud detection rate at 85% specificity on held‑out data. It explains the dataset composition, the modeling goal of ranking claims by risk, and the data preprocessing steps that reduce the feature set from 40 to 35 columns before training.

chunks.content:
**`authorities_contacted`, 91 nulls.** The other levels are Police, Fire, Ambulance and
Other. In the raw CSV these 91 rows say "None", which pandas reads as missing by default,
so they are claims where no authority was contacted. I filled them as their own category.
Dropping them would have cost 9% of a dataset with only 247 fraud cases to learn from.

**`_c39`, 1,000 nulls.** Trailing-comma artefact from the CSV export. Dropped.

**One claim with `umbrella_limit` = -1,000,000.** A coverage ceiling can't be negative.
I removed the row instead of guessing which sign was intended, since one row in a
thousand isn't worth inventing a value for. `capital-loss` was left out of this check
because it is negative by definition.

**`policy_number`, `incident_location`, `insured_zip`.** One distinct value per row
(994 of 999 for `insured_zip`). A model can memorise these but can't generalise from
them, so they were dropped.

**Dates.** `policy_bind_date` and `incident_date` were converted, used to derive
`days_policy_to_incident` and `vehicle_age`, then dropped. A claim that arrives soon
after a policy starts is a common fraud red flag, so the gap was worth keeping as a
feature.

## What the data says

Fraud rate varies a lot across categorical levels, against a base rate of 24.7%. Ranked
by spread:

| Feature | Highest level | Lowest level | Spread |
|---|---|---|---|
| `insured_hobbies` | 90.6% | 7.5% | 83.1 pts |
| `incident_severity` | 60.9% | 6.6% | 54.3 pts |
| `auto_model` | 43.8% | 0.0% | 43.8 pts |
| `incident_state` | 42.1% | 15.1% | 27.0 pts |
| `authorities_contacted` | 31.6% | 8.8% | 22.8 pts |

![Fraud rate by incident severity](images/fraud-rate-severity.png)

Major Damage claims are fraudulent 60.9% of the time (n=192), against 6.6% to 15.0% for
the other three levels. Total Loss, the most severe category, sits at 15.0%, so fraud
does not simply rise with severity.

![Fraud rate by insured hobbies](images/fraud-rate-hobbies.png)

`insured_hobbies` is stranger. Chess and cross-fit have fraud rates of 90.6% and 76.0%
on 32 and 25 training rows, while every other hobby sits between 7.5% and 31.2%.

Playing chess doesn't make anyone commit insurance fraud. This is almost certainly an
artefact of the synthetic data: the generator leaked label information into that column.
I kept it as one binary `high_risk_hobby` flag instead of nineteen dummy columns because
it is predictive on this data, and it ends up with the largest coefficient in the final
model. It would not carry over to real claims, and a production model should not use it.
chunks.contextBlurb: The excerpt explains data cleaning steps and feature engineering for the Fraudulent Claim Detection dataset, including handling missing values, dropping irrelevant columns, and deriving new features such as days between policy start and incident. It also summarizes fraud rate variations across categorical variables and discusses the impact of the synthetic `insured_hobbies` feature on model performance.

chunks.content:
Two redundancies had to be resolved before fitting a linear model:

- `total_claim_amount` is exactly `injury_claim + property_claim + vehicle_claim`
  (verified on every training row; r = 0.984 with `vehicle_claim` alone). Keeping all
  four sends VIF to infinity, so I kept the total, the figure an investigator would quote.
- `months_as_customer` correlates 0.920 with `age`, so `months_as_customer` was dropped.

![Correlation heatmap](images/correlation-heatmap.png)

## Class balance

![Class balance](images/class-balance.png)

24.7% of claims are fraudulent. That is enough imbalance to make accuracy misleading:
predicting "not fraud" for every claim scores 75.3% and catches nothing.

The training set was oversampled to 50/50 with `RandomOverSampler`, taking it from 699
to 1,052 rows. The validation set was left at its natural rate, because a metric measured
on a balanced set would not describe how the model behaves on real claim traffic.

## Feature selection

85 columns after one-hot encoding. RFECV with F1 scoring selected 6.

RFECV picks features by predictive score and ignores p-values, so I checked its picks in
statsmodels: drop the least significant feature if its p-value is above 0.05, refit, and
repeat, then do the same for any VIF above 5. Going one feature at a time matters because
each p-value depends on the other features in the model.

None needed removing. The final model has 6 features, a maximum p-value of 0.0463 and a
maximum VIF of 1.20: the hobby flag, three incident-severity levels (Total Loss, Minor
Damage and Trivial Damage, with Major Damage as the baseline), the handlers-cleaners
occupation and a grouped "other" car make.
chunks.contextBlurb: The excerpt explains the preprocessing steps taken for the Fraudulent Claim Detection project, including resolving multicollinearity, handling class imbalance, and selecting the final six predictive features for the model.

chunks.content:
![Cutoff tradeoff](images/cutoff-tradeoff.png)

Sensitivity and specificity are closest at **0.60**, which is the cutoff used throughout.
With six binary features the model only produces a small set of distinct probabilities, so
cutoffs of 0.6, 0.7 and 0.8 classify every training claim the same way; 0.60 is the
first of the three.

Taking the balance point treats a missed fraud and a wrongly flagged honest claim as
equally costly, and in a real claims operation they aren't. A missed fraud costs the full
payout, while a false flag costs an adjuster's time and some goodwill. An insurer who knew
both costs would move the cutoff, and this curve is what they would use to do it.

![ROC curve](images/roc-curve.png)

## Training set (oversampled to 1,052 rows)

| Model | Accuracy | Sensitivity | Specificity | Precision | F1 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Logistic regression, cutoff 0.5 | 0.875 | 0.901 | 0.850 | 0.857 | 0.879 |
| Logistic regression, cutoff 0.60 | 0.875 | 0.884 | 0.865 | 0.868 | 0.876 |
| Random forest, tuned | 0.982 | 0.998 | 0.966 | 0.967 | 0.982 |

## Validation set (300 claims, natural 24.7% fraud rate)

| Model | Accuracy | Sensitivity | Specificity | Precision | F1 | AUC |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Logistic regression** | **0.847** | **0.838** | **0.850** | **0.646** | **0.729** | **0.855** |
| Random forest (tuned) | 0.813 | 0.730 | 0.841 | 0.600 | 0.659 | 0.825 |

![Validation confusion matrices](images/confusion-matrices-validation.png)

In claim terms: of 74 fraudulent claims in the validation set, logistic regression caught
62 and missed 12. Of the 96 claims it flagged, 34 were honest claims sent for review.
chunks.contextBlurb: The excerpt explains how the chosen cutoff of 0.60 for the logistic regression model balances sensitivity and specificity, and presents performance metrics for both training and validation sets, including confusion matrices and ROC curves. It also discusses the practical cost implications of missed fraud versus false flags in a claims operation.

chunks.content:
**The random forest overfits.** It scores 1.000 on every training metric before tuning
and 0.982 accuracy after, then drops to 0.813 accuracy and F1 0.659 on validation, below
the logistic regression on all six measures. Grid search chose `max_depth=10` and
`min_samples_leaf=1` (the grid also offered depths of 6 and unlimited, and leaf sizes of
3 and 5), and trees that size still fit the oversampled training set almost perfectly.

**The cross-validated scores are inflated.** Cross-validation on the oversampled training
set gave F1 = 0.921 ± 0.005. Oversampling duplicates minority rows before the data is
split into folds, so copies of the same claim end up in a training fold and in the fold
used to test it. The validation set was never resampled, which makes it the only honest
estimate here. The fix is to resample inside each fold.

**The simpler model won, probably because the dataset is small.** With 699 training rows
and 173 fraud cases, six significant coefficients generalised better than 200 depth-10
trees trained on 18 features.

**Part of the signal is an artefact.** `high_risk_hobby` has the largest coefficient and
comes from a leak in the data generator, so performance would likely fall a long way
without it. The validation numbers above overstate what this model would do on real
claims.
chunks.contextBlurb: This excerpt appears in the README of the Fraudulent_Claim_Detection project, where the authors discuss the performance and pitfalls of their random forest model, including overfitting, inflated cross‑validated scores due to oversampling, and the impact of a data leakage feature.

chunks.content:
- 1,000 rows and 247 fraud cases, so every validation metric has a wide confidence
  interval.
- The data is synthetic and contains leaked label information. It can demonstrate the
  method but can't estimate real fraud-detection performance.
- Oversampling before cross-validation inflates the CV-based scores in the notebook
  (RFECV, the cross-validation check and the grid search).
- The split is random. In production you predict future claims from past ones, so a
  time-ordered split would be a harder and fairer test.
- Impurity-based feature importance favours high-cardinality and continuous features, so
  the random forest ranking is not directly comparable to the logistic coefficients.

## Next steps

- Resample inside each CV fold (`imblearn.pipeline.Pipeline`) so the cross-validated
  scores mean something
- Refit without `high_risk_hobby` to see how much of the performance is real
- Set the threshold from costs once the relative cost of a missed fraud and a false flag
  is known
- Try gradient boosting with explicit depth limits, between the two models tried here
- Check calibration, since a risk score that feeds a review queue should be a probability
  an operator can reason about

```
<Figure size 1600x950 with 6 Axes>
```

**Observations:** The share who stayed varies most across:
- Job Level: 36.1% for Entry against 79.3% for Senior, the largest gap of any feature (43.3 points).
- Marital Status: 32.5% of single employees stayed, against 63.8% of married ones.
- Remote Work: 75.4% of remote workers stayed, against 47.1% of everyone else.
- Education Level: 75.0% of PhD holders stayed, while every other level sits at 50 to 51%.
- Work-Life Balance: from 40.0% for Poor up to 64.0% for Excellent.

Company Reputation, Performance Rating, Gender and Job Satisfaction show smaller gaps of 8.4 to 12.8 points, and Overtime 5.6 points. Company Size, Innovation Opportunities, Leadership Opportunities, Employee Recognition and Job Role barely move (3.2 points or less), so they are unlikely to matter much in the model.

Job Satisfaction does not run in order: employees with Very High satisfaction stayed at 46.6%, about the same as Low (46.3%) and well below High (54.7%) and Medium (54.3%). That is hard to explain and may be another sign that the data is synthetic.

**Model Interpretation**

The output summary table  will provide the features used for building model along with coefficient of each of the feature and their p-value. The p-value in a logistic regression model is used to assess the statistical significance of each coefficient. Lesser the p-value, more significant the feature is in the model.

A positive coefficient will indicate that an increase in the value of feature would increase the odds of the event occurring. On the other hand, a negative coefficient means the opposite, i.e,  an increase in the value of feature would decrease the odds of the event occurring.

7.3.1 Plot ROC curve <font color="red">[3 Marks]</font>

```python
# Define ROC function
def draw_roc(actual, probs, title, filename=None):
    fpr, tpr, thresholds = metrics.roc_curve(actual, probs, drop_intermediate=False)
    auc_score = metrics.roc_auc_score(actual, probs)

    plt.figure(figsize=(6, 5.5))
    plt.plot(fpr, tpr, color=blue, linewidth=2, label=f"Logistic regression (AUC = {auc_score:.3f})")
    plt.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], color=grey, linestyle="--", linewidth=1, label="Random guess")
    plt.xlim([0.0, 1.0])
    plt.ylim([0.0, 1.02])
    plt.xlabel("False positive rate (1 - specificity)")
    plt.ylabel("True positive rate (sensitivity)")
    plt.title(title)
    plt.legend(loc="lower right")
    if filename:
        plt.savefig(filename, dpi=150, bbox_inches="tight")
    plt.show()
    return auc_score
```

chunks.content:
After dropping 3,975 rows with missing values and 77 duplicate records, fixing the garbled apostrophes in Education Level and removing `Employee ID`, the model was trained on 49,390 employees and checked on 21,168 it had not seen.

The final model is a logistic regression on the 15 features chosen by RFE. All of them are significant (largest p-value 8.8e-27) and none is collinear with the others (largest VIF 1.84), so no feature had to be removed. With a cutoff of 0.52, where sensitivity and specificity meet on the training data, it scores 0.7394 accuracy, 0.7397 sensitivity, 0.7391 specificity and 0.7553 precision on the validation set, with an AUC of 0.8249. These match the training figures closely, so the model generalises well to new employees.

**What drives retention in this data**, holding the other features fixed:
1. Seniority matters most. Senior staff have about 12 times the odds of staying of entry-level staff, and mid-level staff about 2.6 times.
2. Remote work is the clearest policy lever. Remote workers have about 5.6 times the odds of staying.
3. Work-life balance comes next. Employees who rate it Fair or Poor have roughly a third of the odds of staying of those who rate it Good or Excellent. Overtime lowers the odds too (0.72).
4. Poor or Fair company reputation and Low or Below Average performance ratings also lower the odds (0.48 to 0.72).
5. Gender, marital status and education also appear: men, married or divorced employees and PhD holders are more likely to stay. These help the model predict, but gender and marital status are sensitive characteristics, protected by employment law in many countries, so the model should not be used to treat people differently because of them. They are better read as a prompt to ask why the experience of work differs between these groups.

**Suggestions for HR:**
- Review who can work remotely, since remote workers stay far more often.
- Keep overtime in check, and follow up early on poor work-life balance scores.
- Focus retention effort on entry-level staff, for example through clearer progression to mid-level roles, because they leave the most.
- Use the model as a ranked at-risk list. In the validation data, 72.29% of the employees it flagged as likely to leave did leave.
chunks.contextBlurb: The excerpt summarizes the final logistic regression model built on 49,390 employees after cleaning the dataset, reporting its performance metrics and key predictors of retention such as seniority, remote work, work‑life balance, company reputation, performance, gender, marital status, and education. It also offers HR recommendations based on these findings.

chunks.content:
**Limitations:**
- The data looks synthetic. 40.0% of employees would have joined before 18, Monthly Income contains placeholder values around 50,000, and Very High job satisfaction behaves like Low. The coefficients describe this dataset and may not carry over to a real workforce.
- RFE kept only dummy columns. Because a dummy's coefficient and a standardised column's coefficient are not on the same scale, numerical features such as Distance from Home (rank 3) may have been dropped too early. Testing them in the model, or using a selection method that is not based on coefficient size, is the obvious next step.
- Dropping the rows with missing values removed slightly more stayers than leavers, since employees with a missing tenure stayed more often (62.7% against 52.2%).
- The 0.52 cutoff assumes that both kinds of mistake cost the same.
- The model shows association, not cause. Remote work, for example, may be offered more often to people who were already likely to stay.
chunks.contextBlurb: This excerpt appears in the “Limitations” section of the Jupyter notebook Predicting_Employee_Retention_Shubham_Kumar_Singh.ipynb, where the author discusses data quality, feature selection, handling of missing values, threshold choice, and the distinction between association and causation in the employee retention model.

chunks.content:
Logistic regression on 74,610 employee records to predict who will stay at a mid-sized
technology company, and to show HR which factors go with staying.

**On 21,168 held-out employees the model recognises 74.0% of those who stayed and 73.9% of
those who left (accuracy 0.739, precision 0.755, AUC 0.825), within about half a point of
its training scores.**

## The problem

The company has mostly dealt with attrition after it happens. It wants to know in advance
who is likely to stay, who is not, and what separates the two groups, so that HR can put
retention effort where it is needed.

That asks two things of a model. It has to rank employees by their chance of staying, so HR
can start with the people least likely to stay. And it has to be explainable, because HR
needs to know what the model is reacting to before acting on it. Logistic regression gives
both: a probability for every employee, and coefficients that turn into odds ratios a
non-specialist can follow.

Stayed is the positive class throughout. Sensitivity is the share of stayers the model
recognises, and specificity is the share of leavers it recognises.

## Data

74,610 employees and 24 columns, covering demographics (age, gender, marital status,
dependents, education), the job (role, level, company size, income, tenure, promotions,
overtime, remote work, distance from home, leadership and innovation opportunities) and
ratings (work-life balance, job satisfaction, performance, company reputation,
recognition). The target is `Attrition`, Stayed or Left.

| Step | Rows | Columns |
|---|---|---|
| Raw | 74,610 | 24 |
| After dropping rows with missing values | 70,635 | 24 |
| After dropping 77 duplicate records | 70,558 | 24 |
| After dropping `Employee ID` | 70,558 | 23 |
| Train / validation (70/30, stratified) | 49,390 / 21,168 | 22 features + target |
| After one-hot encoding | 49,390 / 21,168 | 41 features |
chunks.contextBlurb: The excerpt describes a logistic regression model trained on 74,610 employee records from a mid‑sized technology company to predict employee retention, achieving 74.0% sensitivity and 73.9% specificity on a 21,168‑employee hold‑out set, and explains that the model ranks employees by their probability of staying and provides explainable coefficients for HR decision‑making.

chunks.content:
**Missing values, 3,975 rows.** Only two columns have gaps: Distance from Home (1,912 rows,
2.56%) and Company Tenure (In Months) (2,413 rows, 3.23%). The rows were dropped, which
keeps 94.67% of the data. The gaps are not quite random. Employees with a missing tenure
stayed 62.7% of the time against 52.2% for everyone else, so the drop takes out slightly
more stayers than leavers. Imputing was the alternative, but it would have had to happen
after the split so that the fill values came from training data only. With 70,635 rows
left, dropping was simpler and cost little.

**Garbled text in Education Level.** `Bachelorâ€™s Degree` and `Masterâ€™s Degree` are a
curly apostrophe that went through the wrong text encoding (UTF-8 bytes read as
Windows-1252). Replaced with a plain apostrophe. Every categorical column was then checked
for labels that differ only by case or spacing, and there were none.

**77 duplicate records.** Same Employee ID and the same value in every column, so the same
record entered twice. Removed before the split, so no employee can sit in both the training
and the validation set.

**`Employee ID`.** Unique to each employee. Used to confirm the duplicates, then dropped.

**Left alone.** 52 training rows have a monthly income between 50,000 and 50,030, against a
99th percentile of about 12,250, and 17 have 15 dependents when nobody else has more than 6.
They look like placeholder values, but they are 52 and 17 rows out of 49,390, and neither
column makes it into the final model. The data dictionary also uses some level names the
data does not (Below Average and Very Poor where the data has Fair, Very Low where it has
Very High) and describes Overtime as hours when it is Yes/No. The data is consistent with
itself, so the dictionary was treated as out of date.
chunks.contextBlurb: The excerpt appears in the README of the Predicting_Employee_Retention project, detailing data cleaning steps such as handling missing values, correcting garbled text, removing duplicates, and noting inconsistencies between the data dictionary and the actual dataset.

chunks.content:
The share who stayed swings a lot across some categorical features and hardly moves across
others. Ranked by the gap between the highest and lowest level, on the training data, against
an overall rate of 52.1%:

| Feature | Highest level | Lowest level | Gap |
|---|---|---|---|
| Job Level | Senior, 79.3% | Entry, 36.1% | 43.3 pts |
| Marital Status | Married, 63.8% | Single, 32.5% | 31.3 pts |
| Remote Work | Yes, 75.4% | No, 47.1% | 28.3 pts |
| Education Level | PhD, 75.0% | Master's Degree, 50.5% | 24.5 pts |
| Work-Life Balance | Excellent, 64.0% | Poor, 40.0% | 24.1 pts |
| Company Reputation | Good, 56.7% | Poor, 43.9% | 12.8 pts |

At the other end, Job Role (1.6 points), Employee Recognition (2.3), Leadership
Opportunities (3.0), Company Size (3.2) and Innovation Opportunities (3.2) barely move.

![Share of employees who stayed, by category](images/retention-by-category.png)

Job level is the clearest pattern. Entry-level staff leave far more often than senior staff,
with mid-level staff in between. Remote workers stay much more often than everyone else.
Education only matters at the top: PhD holders stand apart, while the other four levels all
sit at 50 to 51%.

Job Satisfaction does not run in order. Employees with Very High satisfaction stayed 46.6%
of the time, about the same as Low (46.3%) and well below Medium (54.3%) and High (54.7%).
There is no sensible story for that, and it is one of several signs that this is synthetic
data. Another is that 40.0% of employees would have joined the company before the age of
18, with the youngest implied joining age at 8.
chunks.contextBlurb: This excerpt appears in the README of the Predicting_Employee_Retention project, where it discusses the distribution of employee retention rates across various categorical features and highlights key patterns such as job level and remote work.

chunks.content:
![Correlation heatmap](images/correlation-heatmap.png)

None of the numerical columns says much on its own. The strongest correlation with staying
is Distance from Home at -0.096, then Number of Promotions (0.077) and Number of Dependents
(0.073). Monthly Income is effectively unrelated (0.009). Among themselves, the only real
correlations are Age with Years at Company (0.53) and Years at Company with Company Tenure
(0.44), which is not high enough to treat either column as redundant.

## Class balance

![Class balance](images/class-balance.png)

52.1% stayed and 47.9% left. That is close enough to balanced that no resampling was
needed, and accuracy is a fair headline number. Sensitivity and specificity are still
reported throughout, because they show how the model treats each group.

## Feature selection

One-hot encoding the 15 categorical columns, dropping the first level of each, gives 34
dummies, and with the 7 numerical columns that makes 41 features. The numerical columns
were standardised with a scaler fitted on the training data only. RFE with a scikit-learn
logistic regression picked 15 features, and a statsmodels GLM with a binomial family was
then fitted on those 15 for p-values, followed by a VIF check.

The rule was to remove one feature at a time, whichever had a p-value above 0.05 or a VIF
above 5, and refit after each removal. Nothing came close to either threshold.

The final model has 15 features, a maximum p-value of 8.8e-27 and a maximum VIF of 1.84.
They are all dummies: Job Level (Mid, Senior), Remote Work, Education Level (PhD),
Gender (Male), Marital Status (Single), Work-Life Balance (Fair, Poor), Company Reputation
(Fair, Poor), Performance Rating (Low, Below Average), Job Satisfaction (Low, Very High) and
Overtime.

With 49,390 training rows, a p-value below 0.05 is an easy bar to clear, so the VIFs and
the validation results carry more weight here than the significance tests.

RFE kept no numerical column at all. Distance from Home ranked 3rd and Number of Promotions
5th, just outside the cut. RFE removes whichever feature has the smallest coefficient, and a
coefficient on a 0/1 dummy is not on the same scale as one on a standardised column, so the
ranking leans towards dummies and some numerical columns may have been dropped too early.
chunks.contextBlurb: This excerpt appears in the README of the Predicting_Employee_Retention project, where it discusses exploratory data analysis, class balance, and the feature selection process for building a logistic regression model to predict employee retention.

chunks.content:
![Cutoff trade-off](images/cutoff-tradeoff.png)

At the default 0.5, sensitivity (0.754) is ahead of specificity (0.720). The curves cross
between 0.5 and 0.6, and a finer search in steps of 0.01 puts the crossing at **0.52**
(sensitivity 0.740, specificity 0.734). Accuracy hardly changes (0.738 at 0.5, 0.737 at
0.52), so moving the cutoff mostly shifts mistakes from one group to the other.

Precision and recall cross at about 0.507, close enough to 0.52 that there was no reason to
adjust it.

The crossover treats the two mistakes as equally costly: telling HR an employee is likely to
stay when they are about to leave, and flagging someone for retention effort who was going
to stay anyway. In practice the first is usually the more expensive one, since replacing a
person costs more than a conversation. With real costs the cutoff would move up, and this
curve is what you would use to move it.

![ROC curve](images/roc-curve.png)

The training AUC is 0.826. Pick one employee who stayed and one who left at random, and the
model gives the stayer the higher probability about 83% of the time.

![Precision and recall](images/precision-recall.png)

## Training set (49,390 employees)

| Cutoff | Accuracy | Sensitivity | Specificity | Precision | Recall | AUC |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0.5 | 0.738 | 0.754 | 0.720 | 0.746 | 0.754 | 0.826 |
| 0.52 | 0.737 | 0.740 | 0.734 | 0.752 | 0.740 | 0.826 |
chunks.contextBlurb: The excerpt is from the README of the Predicting_Employee_Retention project, where it explains how the model’s cutoff threshold affects sensitivity, specificity, precision, recall, and overall accuracy, and shows the ROC and precision‑recall curves along with a table of performance metrics for the training set.

chunks.content:
| Accuracy | Sensitivity | Specificity | Precision | Recall | AUC |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **0.739** | **0.740** | **0.739** | **0.755** | **0.740** | **0.825** |

In employee terms: 10,136 of the validation employees left. The model flagged 10,364 people
as likely to leave, of whom 7,492 did leave and 2,872 stayed, so 72.3% of its at-risk list
was right. It missed 2,644 leavers.

## Findings

![Odds ratios in the final model](images/odds-ratios.png)

**Seniority and remote work matter most.** Holding the other features fixed, senior staff
have 12.05 times the odds of staying of entry-level staff, and mid-level staff 2.64 times.
Remote workers have 5.62 times the odds of those who do not work remotely. Remote work is
also the factor here that HR can change most directly, though the limitations below explain
why 5.62 should not be read as cause and effect.

**Work-life balance comes next.** Rating it Fair or Poor cuts the odds of staying to 0.34
and 0.29 of the Good and Excellent groups. Overtime lowers them to 0.72. A Poor or Fair view
of the company's reputation and a weak performance rating push the same way (0.48 to 0.72).

**Some strong predictors are not things HR should act on.** Single employees have 0.18
times the odds of staying of married or divorced ones, and men have 1.80 times the odds of
women. These help the model rank people, but gender and marital status are protected
characteristics in the employment law of many countries. HR can use them to ask why the
experience of work differs between groups. They should never be the basis for treating an
individual differently.

**The model holds up on new data.** Every validation measure is within about half a point of
the training figure at the same cutoff, for example accuracy 0.739 against 0.737 and AUC
0.825 against 0.826. With 49,390 training rows and 15 features there was little room to
overfit, and there is no sign of it.

**Accuracy tops out at about 74%.** At every cutoff checked between 0.4 and 0.6, training
accuracy stays between 0.729 and 0.738. The remaining errors are employees whose recorded
features look like the other group's, and moving the cutoff only trades one kind of error
for the other. Getting past that would take new information about employees or a model that
can pick up interactions.
chunks.contextBlurb: This table and discussion appear in the README of the Predicting_Employee_Retention project, summarizing the validation performance metrics and key findings of the employee churn model.

chunks.content:
- The data looks synthetic. 40.0% of employees would have joined before 18, Age and Distance
  from Home are spread almost evenly across their ranges, Monthly Income has placeholder
  values near 50,000, and Very High job satisfaction behaves like Low. The coefficients
  describe this dataset and should not be read as facts about real employees.
- RFE ranks features by coefficient size, which favours dummies over standardised numerical
  columns. Distance from Home, ranked 3rd, may belong in the model.
- Dropping the rows with missing values removed slightly more stayers than leavers, because
  employees with a missing tenure stayed more often (62.7% against 52.2%).
- One random split and no cross-validation. 21,168 validation rows keep the sampling error
  small, but it is still a single split.
- The odds ratios show association, not cause. Remote work may be offered more often to
  people who were already likely to stay, so 5.62 is not a forecast of what extending remote
  work would do.
- The 0.52 cutoff assumes both kinds of mistake cost the same.

## Next steps

- Test the numerical features RFE left out, starting with Distance from Home and Number of
  Promotions, or let cross-validation choose the number of features (RFECV) instead of
  fixing it at 15
- Impute tenure and distance on the training data with a "was missing" flag, since the gaps
  carried some signal
- Set the cutoff from real costs once HR can say what a missed leaver costs compared with an
  unnecessary retention conversation
- Try interaction terms (job level by remote work, for example) or a tree-based model to see
  whether the 74% ceiling moves
- Check calibration, so that a predicted 70% chance of staying means roughly 70% in practice

chunks.content:
Answering 29 questions in MySQL about India's crop insurance scheme, Pradhan Mantri Fasal
Bima Yojana (PMFBY), on 1,870 district-year records from 2018 to 2021.

## Executive summary

Madhya Pradesh (9.15 million farmers covered, summed over 2018 to 2021), Maharashtra
(8.94 million), Uttar Pradesh (7.24 million) and Rajasthan (6.82 million) account for
63.9% of all coverage. Madhya Pradesh also has the largest sum insured, ₹84,132 crore or
a quarter of the total, ahead of Rajasthan at ₹53,635 crore.

Farmers paid ₹5,624 crore of the ₹43,007 crore gross premium, or 13.1%. State governments
paid ₹19,740 crore (45.9%) and the central government ₹17,643 crore (41.0%). The farmers'
share fell every year, from 19.1% in 2018 to 10.6% in 2021, while gross premium rose from
₹7,263 crore to ₹13,119 crore.

Coverage fell from 15.0 million farmers in 2018 to 10.8 million in 2021, and the number
of reporting states dropped from 24 to 20. Andhra Pradesh, Gujarat, Jharkhand and
Telangana report only for 2018 and 2019, and West Bengal only for 2018. Each year, the
farmers covered equal 1.41% to 1.63% of the population of the reporting districts.
The highest state-years are Chhattisgarh in 2021 (4.97%) and Tripura in 2020 (4.68%).

Bid in Maharashtra has more farmers covered than any other district (1.43 million) and
the highest single-year farmers' premium (₹72.4 crore in 2019). Its 2019 record also has
the largest sum insured in the data. Bid, Ujjain and Latur are the only districts where
farmers paid more than ₹100 crore in total.

Karnataka's money columns look broken at source: 736,375 farmers covered against a total
sum insured of ₹3.18 lakh.

The queries behind these figures are in `summary_queries.sql`.
chunks.contextBlurb: This excerpt is from the README of the SQL_Farmers_Insurance_Analysis project, summarizing key findings from 29 MySQL queries on PMFBY data for 1,870 district-year records between 2018 and 2021. It highlights coverage, premium contributions, and state-level variations, and references the `summary_queries.sql` file for the underlying queries.

chunks.content:
- Money columns are in lakh rupees (scaling factor 100,000 in `column_description.csv`).
  So 500,000 rupees in Q9 means `SumInsured > 5`, 20 crore in Q17 is 2,000 lakh and
  100 crore in Q18 is 10,000 lakh.
- `Year` is a text label such as "Calendar Year (Jan - Dec), 2020", so every year filter
  uses the numeric `srcYear`, Q3 and Q29 included.
- Five district names (Balrampur, Bilaspur, Hamirpur, Pratapgarh, Raigarh) exist in two
  states, so districts are always grouped together with their state.
- A row is one district in one year. Q11 and Q19 compare rows. Q20 and Q23 use totals
  over all years; row by row, Q20 would return nothing, because the record with the
  highest premium (Bid, 2019) also has the largest sum insured.
- Q12 follows the course brief, which asks for the top 3 states in each year, ranked by
  farmers covered as a percentage of population. Sorted by that figure, the first three
  rows are also the overall top 3 that the question file asks for.
- Q16's INNER JOIN is a self-join on state, district and year, so only years with more
  than 10 insurance units count. Joining on state and district alone repeats each row once
  per year and would put Bid at ₹581 crore instead of ₹145 crore.
- Q17 reports the year and population of each district's peak year.
- `TotalPopulation` repeats a Census figure every year, so Q21 compares states within a
  single year; summing across years would count each district up to four times. Uttar
  Pradesh comes out on top either way.
- Q24's running total is partitioned by state and district.
- 13 district codes carry more than one name (Tamil Nadu's 2021 "I" and "II" splits,
  Assam codes reused in 2021, and a few clashes elsewhere), so a plain `SELECT DISTINCT`
  would break the `districts` primary key. Each code keeps its most frequent name, newest
  year first on ties, which gives 555 districts.
- Q28 changes only the `Year` text. Q29 then deletes 190 rows from 2020, including six
  from Himachal Pradesh and rowID 1, the record Q27 had just updated.
chunks.contextBlurb: This excerpt explains how the README for the SQL_Farmers_Insurance_Analysis project describes the data scaling, year labeling, district grouping, query logic, and specific query behaviors such as Q20, Q12, Q16, Q17, Q21, Q24, and Q28/Q29.

chunks.content:
The course's copy of the data is derived from the PMFBY figures on the National Data and
Analytics Platform (NDAP). `data.csv` has 1,870 rows and 44 columns. Each row is one
district in one year and holds the PMFBY figures (insurance units, farmers covered,
loanee and non-loanee applications, insured area, the three premium parts, gross
premium, sum insured and the farmer mix in percent) next to Census figures for the
district (population by sex and urban or rural, households, land area).

It covers 27 states and union territories and 565 state and district pairs, but not
every state reports every year: 525 rows in 2018, 505 in 2019, 429 in 2020 and 411 in
2021. Money is in lakh rupees (1 lakh = 100,000 rupees, 100 lakh = 1 crore) and
`InsuredLandArea` is in thousand hectares. The summary above converts money to crore.

Blank fields become NULL during the load, through `NULLIF(@x, '')` in `setup.sql`. Only
two groups of columns have blanks. The ten percentage columns are blank in 21 rows, which
are exactly the 21 rows where no farmers were covered (all in Karnataka), so the shares
are undefined there and stay NULL. The Census land-area columns are blank in 2, 28 and 29
rows. Every column the questions filter or aggregate on is complete, and `NOT NULL`
constraints hold it to that, so the aggregates need no `IFNULL` padding. `COALESCE`
handles the outer join in Q18 and `NULLIF` guards the division in Q12.

Karnataka's premiums and sums insured are far too small for the number of farmers it
reports, which is why Karnataka fills the Q11 list and drops out of Q9. `DistrictCode` is
also unreliable as a key (see Assumptions).
chunks.contextBlurb: This excerpt explains the structure and contents of the `data.csv` file used in the SQL Farmers Insurance Analysis project, detailing how the PMFBY and Census data are combined, the handling of missing values, and specific issues with Karnataka data. It also notes the file’s size, coverage across states and years, and the data types for monetary and land area fields.

chunks.content:
The 29 questions follow the course's ten sections:

| Section | Questions | What the SQL does |
|---|---|---|
| Select and filter | Q1 to Q6 | `DISTINCT`, `WHERE` on text and numbers, totals per state and per district |
| Aggregation | Q7 to Q9 | `AVG` and `SUM` with `GROUP BY`, the lakh conversion in Q9 |
| Sorting | Q10 to Q12 | `ORDER BY ... LIMIT`, a derived table that picks rows before sorting them (Q11), CTEs with `ROW_NUMBER()` for a top 3 per year (Q12) |
| String functions | Q13 to Q15 | `LEFT()`, `LIKE 'B%'` and `LIKE '%pur'` |
| Joins | Q16 to Q18 | a self-join on the natural key, a join back to a grouped derived table, a `LEFT JOIN` of two district-level aggregates |
| Subqueries | Q19 to Q21 | scalar subqueries in `WHERE` and `HAVING`, nested two deep in Q21 |
| Window functions | Q22 to Q24 | `ROW_NUMBER()`, `RANK()` over grouped totals, a running `SUM()` with an explicit frame |
| Constraints | Q25 and Q26 | primary, unique and foreign keys with `ON UPDATE CASCADE` and `ON DELETE RESTRICT`, filled with `INSERT ... SELECT` |
| Updates and deletes | Q27 to Q29 | keyed `UPDATE` and `DELETE`, kept last so they cannot change earlier answers |

Q12 ranks states inside each year with a window function over a grouped CTE:

```sql
WITH state_year_coverage AS (
    SELECT
        srcStateName,
        srcYear,
        100 * SUM(TotalFarmersCovered) / NULLIF(SUM(TotalPopulation), 0) AS farmers_to_population_pct
    FROM FarmersInsuranceData
    GROUP BY srcStateName, srcYear
),
ranked_states AS (
    SELECT
        srcStateName,
        srcYear,
        farmers_to_population_pct,
        ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY srcYear ORDER BY farmers_to_population_pct DESC, srcStateName) AS rank_in_year
    FROM state_year_coverage
)
SELECT
    srcStateName,
    srcYear,
    farmers_to_population_pct,
    rank_in_year
FROM ranked_states
WHERE rank_in_year <= 3
ORDER BY farmers_to_population_pct DESC;
```

Q17 finds each district's peak premium in a grouped derived table, then joins back to the
base rows to recover the year it happened:

```sql
SELECT
    records.srcStateName,
    records.srcDistrictName,
    records.Year,
    records.TotalPopulation,
    peaks.max_farmers_premium_lakh
FROM FarmersInsuranceData AS records
INNER JOIN (
    SELECT
        srcStateName,
        srcDistrictName,
        MAX(FarmersPremiumAmount) AS max_farmers_premium_lakh
    FROM FarmersInsuranceData
    GROUP BY srcStateName, srcDistrictName
    HAVING MAX(FarmersPremiumAmount) > 2000
) AS peaks
    ON  peaks.srcStateName             = records.srcStateName
    AND peaks.srcDistrictName          = records.srcDistrictName
    AND peaks.max_farmers_premium_lakh = records.FarmersPremiumAmount
ORDER BY peaks.max_farmers_premium_lakh DESC;
```
chunks.contextBlurb: This excerpt is from the README of the SQL_Farmers_Insurance_Analysis project, detailing the 29 SQL questions organized by topic and providing example queries for Q12 and Q17.

chunks.content:
The table has a primary key on `rowID` and a unique key on (`srcStateName`,
`srcDistrictName`, `srcYear`), which enforces one row per district per year and doubles
as the index for state filters, `DISTINCT` states and the district-level joins. Two more
indexes cover year filters and premium lookups. The `EXPLAIN` in Q17 shows the derived
table grouped straight off the unique key and each peak matched back through
`idx_farmers_premium`. All three data changes in Q27 to Q29 go through an index, so they
also run under MySQL Workbench's safe update mode.

The solution file runs top to bottom on a fresh load with no errors or warnings. As a
cross-check I recomputed every result except the Q25 table definitions in pandas from
the CSV, and they all matched.
chunks.contextBlurb: The excerpt explains the indexing strategy and query performance details for the Farmers Insurance dataset, noting how the primary key, unique key, and additional indexes support efficient filtering, grouping, and updates, and confirms that the provided solution script runs correctly on a fresh load.

chunks.content:
MySQL 8.0.16 or later (window functions, CTEs and `EXPLAIN FORMAT=TREE`).

```bash
# Allow local file loads on the server (once, needs admin rights)
mysql -u root -p -e "SET GLOBAL local_infile = 1;"

# From the repository root, so the relative path data/data.csv resolves
mysql --local-infile=1 -u root -p < setup.sql
mysql -u root -p < summary_queries.sql
mysql -u root -p < SQL_Farmers_Insurance_Analysis_Shubham_Kumar_Singh.sql
```

The CSV files are course material and are not committed: put `data.csv` and
`column_description.csv` in `data/` first. Q27 to Q29 change the data, so run `setup.sql`
again before a second run. In MySQL Workbench, the load also needs `OPT_LOCAL_INFILE=1`
under the connection's Advanced options and an absolute path to `data.csv` in
`setup.sql`, because Workbench does not start in the repository folder.

```sql
-- Farmers' Insurance Analysis (PMFBY data) in MySQL 8
-- Shubham Kumar Singh
-- Run setup.sql first. Q27 to Q29 change the data, so reload with setup.sql before running this file again.

USE ndap;
```

## Section 1: SELECT Queries

```sql
-- ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- SECTION 1. 
-- SELECT Queries [5 Marks]

-- 	Q1.	Retrieve the names of all states (srcStateName) from the dataset.
-- ###
-- 	[2 Marks]
-- ###
-- TYPE YOUR CODE BELOW >
-- <write your answers in the empty spaces given, the length of solution queries (and the solution writing space) can vary>
SELECT DISTINCT srcStateName
FROM FarmersInsuranceData
ORDER BY srcStateName;

###

-- 	Q2.	Retrieve the total number of farmers covered (TotalFarmersCovered) 
-- 		and the sum insured (SumInsured) for each state (srcStateName), ordered by TotalFarmersCovered in descending order.
-- ###
-- 	[3 Marks]

    srcStateName,
    SUM(TotalFarmersCovered) AS total_farmers_covered,
```

chunks.content:
```sql
-- --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- SECTION 2. 
-- Filtering Data (WHERE) [15 Marks]

-- 	Q3.	Retrieve all records where Year is '2020'.
-- ###
-- 	[2 Marks]
-- ###
-- TYPE YOUR CODE BELOW >
-- Assumption: Year holds a text label ('Calendar Year (Jan - Dec), 2020'), so year filters here and below use the numeric srcYear.
SELECT *

-- ###

-- 	Q4.	Retrieve all rows where the TotalPopulationRural is greater than 1 million and the srcStateName is 'HIMACHAL PRADESH'.
```

chunks.content:
```sql
-- ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

-- SECTION 3.
-- Aggregation (GROUP BY) [10 marks]

-- 	Q7. 	Calculate the average insured land area (InsuredLandArea) for each year (srcYear).
-- ###
-- 	[3 Marks]
-- ###
-- TYPE YOUR CODE BELOW >
SELECT
    srcYear,
    ROUND(AVG(InsuredLandArea), 2) AS avg_insured_land_area_thousand_ha
FROM FarmersInsuranceData
GROUP BY srcYear
ORDER BY srcYear;

-- ###

-- 	Q8. 	Calculate the total number of farmers covered (TotalFarmersCovered) for each district (srcDistrictName) where Insurance units is greater than 0.
-- ###
-- 	[3 Marks]
-- ###
-- TYPE YOUR CODE BELOW >
-- Assumption: districts are grouped together with their state, because five district names (Bilaspur, Hamirpur and others) exist in two states.
SELECT
    srcStateName,
    srcDistrictName,
    SUM(TotalFarmersCovered) AS total_farmers_covered
FROM FarmersInsuranceData
WHERE InsuranceUnits > 0
GROUP BY srcStateName, srcDistrictName
ORDER BY total_farmers_covered DESC, srcStateName, srcDistrictName;

-- ###

-- 	Q9.	For each state (srcStateName), calculate the total premium amounts (FarmersPremiumAmount, StatePremiumAmount, GOVPremiumAmount) 
-- 		and the total number of farmers covered (TotalFarmersCovered). Only include records where the sum insured (SumInsured) is greater than 500,000 (remember to check for scaling).
-- ###
-- 	[4 Marks]
-- ###
-- TYPE YOUR CODE BELOW >
-- Assumption: SumInsured is in lakh INR (scaling factor 100,000), so 500,000 rupees means SumInsured > 5.
SELECT
    srcStateName,
    SUM(FarmersPremiumAmount) AS total_farmers_premium_lakh,
    SUM(StatePremiumAmount)   AS total_state_premium_lakh,
    SUM(GOVPremiumAmount)     AS total_gov_premium_lakh,
    SUM(TotalFarmersCovered)  AS total_farmers_covered
FROM FarmersInsuranceData
WHERE SumInsured > 5
GROUP BY srcStateName
ORDER BY srcStateName;

-- ###
```

chunks.content:
```sql
-- -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- SECTION 4.
-- Sorting Data (ORDER BY) [10 Marks]

-- 	Q10.	Retrieve the top 5 districts (srcDistrictName) with the highest TotalPopulation in the year 2020.
-- ###
-- 	[2 Marks]
-- ###
-- TYPE YOUR CODE BELOW >
SELECT
    srcStateName,
    srcDistrictName,
    TotalPopulation
FROM FarmersInsuranceData
WHERE srcYear = 2020
ORDER BY TotalPopulation DESC
LIMIT 5;

-- ###

-- 	Q11.	Retrieve the srcStateName, srcDistrictName, and SumInsured for the 10 districts with the lowest non-zero FarmersPremiumAmount, 
-- 		ordered by insured sum and then the FarmersPremiumAmount.
-- ###
-- 	[3 Marks]
-- ###
-- TYPE YOUR CODE BELOW >
-- Assumption: rows are district-years, so the 10 lowest non-zero premiums are taken first (a district can appear for two years) and then sorted as asked.
SELECT
    srcStateName,
    srcDistrictName,
    SumInsured,
    srcYear,
    FarmersPremiumAmount
FROM (
    SELECT
        srcStateName,
        srcDistrictName,
        SumInsured,
        srcYear,
        FarmersPremiumAmount
    FROM FarmersInsuranceData
    WHERE FarmersPremiumAmount > 0
    ORDER BY FarmersPremiumAmount ASC, SumInsured ASC
    LIMIT 10
) AS lowest_premiums
ORDER BY SumInsured ASC, FarmersPremiumAmount ASC;

###

-- 	Q12. 	Retrieve the top 3 states (srcStateName) along with the year (srcYear) where the ratio of insured farmers (TotalFarmersCovered) to the total population (TotalPopulation) is highest. 
-- 		Sort the results by the ratio in descending order.
-- ###
-- 	[5 Marks]
-- ###
-- TYPE YOUR CODE BELOW >
-- Assumption: read as the top 3 states in each year, ranked on SUM(TotalFarmersCovered) / SUM(TotalPopulation) shown as a percentage; the first 3 rows are also the overall top 3.
WITH state_year_coverage AS (
    SELECT
        srcStateName,
        srcYear,
        100 * SUM(TotalFarmersCovered) / NULLIF(SUM(TotalPopulation), 0) AS farmers_to_population_pct
    FROM FarmersInsuranceData
    GROUP BY srcStateName, srcYear
),
ranked_states AS (
    SELECT
        srcStateName,
        srcYear,
        farmers_to_population_pct,
        ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY srcYear ORDER BY farmers_to_population_pct DESC, srcStateName) AS rank_in_year
    FROM state_year_coverage
)
SELECT
    srcStateName,
    srcYear,
    farmers_to_population_pct,
    rank_in_year
FROM ranked_states
WHERE rank_in_year <= 3
ORDER BY farmers_to_population_pct DESC;

-- ###
```

```sql
-- -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

-- SECTION 5.
-- String Functions [6 Marks]

-- 	Q13. 	Create StateShortName by retrieving the first 3 characters of the srcStateName for each unique state.
-- ###
-- 	[2 Marks]
-- ###
```

```sql
-- -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

-- SECTION 6.
-- Joins [14 Marks]

-- 	Q16. 	Perform an INNER JOIN between the srcStateName and srcDistrictName columns to retrieve the aggregated FarmersPremiumAmount for districts where the district’s Insurance units for an individual year are greater than 10.
-- ###
-- 	[4 Marks]
-- ###
-- TYPE YOUR CODE BELOW >
-- Assumption: a self-join that pairs each district-year with itself on state, district and year, so only years with more than 10 insurance units are summed and nothing is counted twice.
SELECT
    premiums.srcStateName,
    premiums.srcDistrictName,
    SUM(premiums.FarmersPremiumAmount) AS total_farmers_premium_lakh
FROM FarmersInsuranceData AS premiums
INNER JOIN FarmersInsuranceData AS units
    ON  units.srcStateName    = premiums.srcStateName
    AND units.srcDistrictName = premiums.srcDistrictName
    AND units.srcYear         = premiums.srcYear
WHERE units.InsuranceUnits > 10
GROUP BY premiums.srcStateName, premiums.srcDistrictName
ORDER BY total_farmers_premium_lakh DESC, premiums.srcStateName, premiums.srcDistrictName;

-- ###

-- 	Q17.	Write a query that retrieves srcStateName, srcDistrictName, Year, TotalPopulation for each district and the the highest recorded FarmersPremiumAmount for that district over all available years
-- 		Return only those districts where the highest FarmersPremiumAmount exceeds 20 crores.
-- ###
-- 	[5 Marks]
-- ###
-- TYPE YOUR CODE BELOW >
-- Assumption: 20 crore = 2,000 lakh; Year and TotalPopulation come from the year in which the district's highest premium was recorded.
SELECT
    records.srcStateName,
    records.srcDistrictName,
    records.Year,
    records.TotalPopulation,
    peaks.max_farmers_premium_lakh
FROM FarmersInsuranceData AS records
INNER JOIN (
    SELECT
        srcStateName,
        srcDistrictName,
        MAX(FarmersPremiumAmount) AS max_farmers_premium_lakh
    FROM FarmersInsuranceData
    GROUP BY srcStateName, srcDistrictName
    HAVING MAX(FarmersPremiumAmount) > 2000
) AS peaks
    ON  peaks.srcStateName             = records.srcStateName
    AND peaks.srcDistrictName          = records.srcDistrictName
    AND peaks.max_farmers_premium_lakh = records.FarmersPremiumAmount
ORDER BY peaks.max_farmers_premium_lakh DESC;

-- Plan check: the peaks table is grouped straight off an ordered scan of uq_state_district_year, and each peak is matched back through idx_farmers_premium.
EXPLAIN FORMAT=TREE
SELECT
    records.srcStateName,
    records.srcDistrictName,
    records.Year,
    records.TotalPopulation,
    peaks.max_farmers_premium_lakh
FROM FarmersInsuranceData AS records
INNER JOIN (
    SELECT
        srcStateName,
        srcDistrictName,
        MAX(FarmersPremiumAmount) AS max_farmers_premium_lakh
    FROM FarmersInsuranceData
    GROUP BY srcStateName, srcDistrictName
    HAVING MAX(FarmersPremiumAmount) > 2000
) AS peaks
    ON  peaks.srcStateName             = records.srcStateName
    AND peaks.srcDistrictName          = records.srcDistrictName
    AND peaks.max_farmers_premium_lakh = records.FarmersPremiumAmount
ORDER BY peaks.max_farmers_premium_lakh DESC;

-- ###

-- 	Q18.	Perform a LEFT JOIN to combine the total population statistics with the farmers’ data (TotalFarmersCovered, SumInsured) for each district and state. 
-- 		Return the total premium amount (FarmersPremiumAmount) and the average population count for each district aggregated over the years, where the total FarmersPremiumAmount is greater than 100 crores.
-- 		Sort the results by total farmers' premium amount, highest first.
-- ###
-- 	[5 Marks]
-- ###
-- TYPE YOUR CODE BELOW >
-- Assumption: 100 crore = 10,000 lakh; both sides are aggregated per district before the join, so no year is counted twice.
SELECT
    population.srcStateName,
    population.srcDistrictName,
    farmers.total_farmers_covered,
    farmers.total_sum_insured_lakh,
    farmers.total_farmers_premium_lakh,
    population.avg_population
FROM (
    SELECT
        srcStateName,
        srcDistrictName,
        ROUND(AVG(TotalPopulation)) AS avg_population
    FROM FarmersInsuranceData
    GROUP BY srcStateName, srcDistrictName
) AS population
LEFT JOIN (
    SELECT
        srcStateName,
        srcDistrictName,
        SUM(TotalFarmersCovered)  AS total_farmers_covered,
        SUM(SumInsured)           AS total_sum_insured_lakh,
        SUM(FarmersPremiumAmount) AS total_farmers_premium_lakh
    FROM FarmersInsuranceData
    GROUP BY srcStateName, srcDistrictName
) AS farmers
    ON  farmers.srcStateName    = population.srcStateName
    AND farmers.srcDistrictName = population.srcDistrictName
WHERE COALESCE(farmers.total_farmers_premium_lakh, 0) > 10000
ORDER BY farmers.total_farmers_premium_lakh DESC;

-- ###
```

```sql
-- SECTION 7.
-- Subqueries [10 Marks]

-- 	Q19.	Write a query to find the districts (srcDistrictName) where the TotalFarmersCovered is greater than the average TotalFarmersCovered across all records.
-- ###
-- 	[2 Marks]
-- ###
-- TYPE YOUR CODE BELOW >
-- Assumption: the comparison is record by record, so a district is listed if any one of its years is above the average.
SELECT DISTINCT
    srcStateName,
    srcDistrictName
FROM FarmersInsuranceData
WHERE TotalFarmersCovered > (
    SELECT AVG(TotalFarmersCovered)
    FROM FarmersInsuranceData
)
ORDER BY srcStateName, srcDistrictName;

-- ###

-- 	Q20.	Write a query to find the srcStateName where the SumInsured is higher than the SumInsured of the district with the highest FarmersPremiumAmount.
-- ###
-- 	[3 Marks]
-- ###
-- TYPE YOUR CODE BELOW >
-- Assumption: states and districts are compared on totals over all years; record by record nothing qualifies, because the top-premium row (Bid, 2019) also has the largest SumInsured.
SELECT
    srcStateName,
    SUM(SumInsured) AS total_sum_insured_lakh
FROM FarmersInsuranceData
GROUP BY srcStateName
HAVING SUM(SumInsured) > (
    SELECT SUM(SumInsured)
    FROM FarmersInsuranceData
    GROUP BY srcStateName, srcDistrictName
    ORDER BY SUM(FarmersPremiumAmount) DESC
    LIMIT 1
)
ORDER BY total_sum_insured_lakh DESC;

-- ###

-- 	Q21.	Write a query to find the srcDistrictName where the FarmersPremiumAmount is higher than the average FarmersPremiumAmount of the state that has the highest TotalPopulation.
-- ###
-- 	[5 Marks]
-- ###
-- TYPE YOUR CODE BELOW >
-- Assumption: TotalPopulation repeats the Census figure every year, so the most populous state is picked within a single year instead of summing across years.
SELECT DISTINCT
    srcStateName,
    srcDistrictName
FROM FarmersInsuranceData
WHERE FarmersPremiumAmount > (
    SELECT AVG(FarmersPremiumAmount)
    FROM FarmersInsuranceData
    WHERE srcStateName = (
        SELECT srcStateName
        FROM FarmersInsuranceData
        GROUP BY srcStateName, srcYear
        ORDER BY SUM(TotalPopulation) DESC
        LIMIT 1
    )
)
ORDER BY srcStateName, srcDistrictName;

-- ###
```

```sql
-- Assumption: each district is ranked on its SumInsured totalled over all years.
SELECT
    srcStateName,

    RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY srcStateName ORDER BY SUM(SumInsured) DESC) AS sum_insured_rank

ORDER BY srcStateName, sum_insured_rank, srcDistrictName;

-- 	Q24.	Use the SUM() window function to calculate a cumulative sum of FarmersPremiumAmount for each district (srcDistrictName), ordered ascending by the srcYear, partitioned by srcStateName.
-- ###
-- 	[4 Marks]

-- TYPE YOUR CODE BELOW >
-- Assumption: the window is partitioned by state and district, so each district gets its own running total (district names repeat across states).
SELECT

    srcDistrictName,
    srcYear,
    FarmersPremiumAmount,
    SUM(FarmersPremiumAmount) OVER (
        PARTITION BY srcStateName, srcDistrictName

FROM FarmersInsuranceData
```

```sql
-- -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

-- SECTION 9.
-- Data Integrity (Constraints, Foreign Keys) [4 Marks]

-- 	Q25.	Create a table 'districts' with DistrictCode as the primary key and columns for DistrictName and StateCode. 
-- 		Create another table 'states' with StateCode as primary key and column for StateName.
-- ###
-- 	[2 Marks]
-- ###
-- TYPE YOUR CODE BELOW >
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS districts, states;

CREATE TABLE states (
    StateCode SMALLINT    NOT NULL,
    StateName VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,
    PRIMARY KEY (StateCode),
    UNIQUE KEY uq_states_state_name (StateName)
);

CREATE TABLE districts (
    DistrictCode SMALLINT    NOT NULL,
    DistrictName VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,
    StateCode    SMALLINT    NOT NULL,
    PRIMARY KEY (DistrictCode)
);

-- ###

-- 	Q26.	Add a foreign key constraint to the districts table that references the StateCode column from a states table.
-- ###
-- 	[2 Marks]
-- ###
-- TYPE YOUR CODE BELOW >
-- A state's code changes flow through to its districts; a state that still has districts cannot be deleted.
ALTER TABLE districts
    ADD CONSTRAINT fk_districts_states
    FOREIGN KEY (StateCode) REFERENCES states (StateCode)
    ON UPDATE CASCADE
    ON DELETE RESTRICT;

-- Load both tables from the main table, states first; every district row is now checked by the foreign key.
INSERT INTO states (StateCode, StateName)
SELECT DISTINCT
    StateCode,
    srcStateName
FROM FarmersInsuranceData;

-- Assumption: 13 DistrictCodes carry more than one name (for example 2021's 'Thanjavur I' and 'Thanjavur II'), so each code keeps its most frequent name, newest year first on ties.
INSERT INTO districts (DistrictCode, DistrictName, StateCode)
SELECT
    DistrictCode,
    srcDistrictName,
    StateCode
FROM (
    SELECT
        DistrictCode,
        srcDistrictName,
        StateCode,
        ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
            PARTITION BY DistrictCode
            ORDER BY COUNT(*) DESC, MAX(srcYear) DESC, srcDistrictName
        ) AS name_rank
    FROM FarmersInsuranceData
    GROUP BY DistrictCode, srcDistrictName, StateCode
) AS ranked_names
WHERE name_rank = 1;

-- Check: 27 states, 555 districts, and every district finds its state.
SELECT
    (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM states)    AS state_rows,
    (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM districts) AS district_rows,
    (SELECT COUNT(*)
     FROM districts
     INNER JOIN states
         ON states.StateCode = districts.StateCode) AS districts_with_state;

-- The constraint at work (left commented out so the script runs end to end):
-- INSERT INTO districts VALUES (999, 'Nowhere', 99);   -- ERROR 1452: no state 99
-- DELETE FROM states WHERE StateCode = 2;              -- ERROR 1451: Himachal Pradesh still has districts

-- ###
```

```sql
-- Farmers' Insurance Analysis (PMFBY): schema, table, data load and indexes.
-- Run it from the repository root so the relative path to data/data.csv resolves:
--     mysql --local-infile=1 -u root -p < setup.sql
-- The server has to allow local loads as well: SET GLOBAL local_infile = 1;

CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS ndap;
USE ndap;

DROP TABLE IF EXISTS FarmersInsuranceData;

-- Column names follow the course starter. Money columns are in lakh INR
-- (1 lakh = 100,000 rupees) and InsuredLandArea is in thousand hectares,
-- as listed in data/column_description.csv.
CREATE TABLE FarmersInsuranceData (
    rowID                           INT           NOT NULL,
    srcYear                         SMALLINT      NOT NULL,
    srcStateName                    VARCHAR(50)   NOT NULL,
    srcDistrictName                 VARCHAR(50)   NOT NULL,
    InsuranceUnits                  INT           NOT NULL,
    TotalFarmersCovered             INT           NOT NULL,
    ApplicationsLoaneeFarmers       INT           NOT NULL,
    ApplicationsNonLoaneeFarmers    INT           NOT NULL,
    InsuredLandArea                 DECIMAL(8,2)  NOT NULL,
    FarmersPremiumAmount            DECIMAL(12,4) NOT NULL,
    StatePremiumAmount              DECIMAL(12,4) NOT NULL,
    GOVPremiumAmount                DECIMAL(12,4) NOT NULL,
    GrossPremiumAmountToBePaid      DECIMAL(12,4) NOT NULL,
    SumInsured                      DECIMAL(12,4) NOT NULL,
    PercentageMaleFarmersCovered    DECIMAL(5,2),
    PercentageFemaleFarmersCovered  DECIMAL(5,2),
    PercentageOthersCovered         DECIMAL(5,2),
    PercentageSCFarmersCovered      DECIMAL(5,2),
    PercentageSTFarmersCovered      DECIMAL(5,2),
    PercentageOBCFarmersCovered     DECIMAL(5,2),
    PercentageGeneralFarmersCovered DECIMAL(5,2),
    PercentageMarginalFarmers       DECIMAL(5,2),
    PercentageSmallFarmers          DECIMAL(5,2),
    PercentageOtherFarmers          DECIMAL(5,2),
    YearCode                        SMALLINT      NOT NULL,
    Year                            VARCHAR(40)   NOT NULL,  -- text label, e.g. 'Calendar Year (Jan - Dec), 2020'
    Country                         VARCHAR(20)   NOT NULL,
    StateCode                       SMALLINT      NOT NULL,
    DistrictCode                    SMALLINT      NOT NULL,
    TotalPopulation                 INT           NOT NULL,
    TotalPopulationUrban            INT           NOT NULL,
    TotalPopulationRural            INT           NOT NULL,
    TotalPopulationMale             INT           NOT NULL,
    TotalPopulationMaleUrban        INT           NOT NULL,
    TotalPopulationMaleRural        INT           NOT NULL,
    TotalPopulationFemale           INT           NOT NULL,
    TotalPopulationFemaleUrban      INT           NOT NULL,
    TotalPopulationFemaleRural      INT           NOT NULL,
    NumberOfHouseholds              INT           NOT NULL,
    NumberOfHouseholdsUrban         INT           NOT NULL,
    NumberOfHouseholdsRural         INT           NOT NULL,
    LandAreaUrban                   DOUBLE,                  -- census areas in hectares, stored as given
    LandAreaRural                   DOUBLE,
    LandArea                        DOUBLE,
    PRIMARY KEY (rowID),
    UNIQUE KEY uq_state_district_year (srcStateName, srcDistrictName, srcYear)  -- one row per district per year
);

-- Blank fields arrive as '' and NULLIF turns them into NULL. Only the
-- percentage and land-area columns have blanks; every other column is complete.
-- The file has Windows line endings, so the last field also loses its '\r'.
LOAD DATA LOCAL INFILE 'data/data.csv'
INTO TABLE FarmersInsuranceData
CHARACTER SET utf8mb4
FIELDS TERMINATED BY ',' OPTIONALLY ENCLOSED BY '"'
LINES TERMINATED BY '\n'
IGNORE 1 LINES
(rowID, srcYear, srcStateName, srcDistrictName, InsuranceUnits, TotalFarmersCovered,
 ApplicationsLoaneeFarmers, ApplicationsNonLoaneeFarmers, InsuredLandArea,
 FarmersPremiumAmount, StatePremiumAmount, GOVPremiumAmount,
 GrossPremiumAmountToBePaid, SumInsured,
 @pct_male, @pct_female, @pct_others, @pct_sc, @pct_st, @pct_obc, @pct_general,
 @pct_marginal, @pct_small, @pct_other_farmers,
 YearCode, Year, Country, StateCode, DistrictCode,
 TotalPopulation, TotalPopulationUrban, TotalPopulationRural,
 TotalPopulationMale, TotalPopulationMaleUrban, TotalPopulationMaleRural,
 TotalPopulationFemale, TotalPopulationFemaleUrban, TotalPopulationFemaleRural,
 NumberOfHouseholds, NumberOfHouseholdsUrban, NumberOfHouseholdsRural,
 @land_area_urban, @land_area_rural, @land_area)
SET PercentageMaleFarmersCovered    = NULLIF(@pct_male, ''),
    PercentageFemaleFarmersCovered  = NULLIF(@pct_female, ''),
    PercentageOthersCovered         = NULLIF(@pct_others, ''),
    PercentageSCFarmersCovered      = NULLIF(@pct_sc, ''),
    PercentageSTFarmersCovered      = NULLIF(@pct_st, ''),
    PercentageOBCFarmersCovered     = NULLIF(@pct_obc, ''),
    PercentageGeneralFarmersCovered = NULLIF(@pct_general, ''),
    PercentageMarginalFarmers       = NULLIF(@pct_marginal, ''),
    PercentageSmallFarmers          = NULLIF(@pct_small, ''),
    PercentageOtherFarmers          = NULLIF(@pct_other_farmers, ''),
    LandAreaUrban                   = NULLIF(@land_area_urban, ''),
    LandAreaRural                   = NULLIF(@land_area_rural, ''),
    LandArea                        = NULLIF(TRIM(TRAILING '\r' FROM @land_area), '');

SHOW WARNINGS;

-- Secondary indexes, built after the bulk load. The unique key above already
-- serves the state filters (Q4, Q21, Q28), DISTINCT states (Q1) and the
-- district-level joins in Q16 and Q17.
CREATE INDEX idx_src_year        ON FarmersInsuranceData (srcYear);               -- year filters: Q3, Q5, Q6, Q10, Q29
CREATE INDEX idx_farmers_premium ON FarmersInsuranceData (FarmersPremiumAmount);  -- Q17 matches each peak premium back to its row

-- Expect 1,870 rows: 21 without the percentage breakdown and 29 without LandArea.
SELECT
    COUNT(*)                                  AS rows_loaded,
    SUM(PercentageMaleFarmersCovered IS NULL) AS rows_without_percentages,
    SUM(LandArea IS NULL)                     AS rows_without_land_area
FROM FarmersInsuranceData;
```

```sql
-- Queries behind the numbers in the README's executive summary. Run after setup.sql, before the solution file changes the data.

USE ndap;

-- Farmers covered per state over 2018 to 2021 (9.15, 8.94, 7.24 and 6.82 million); the fourth running share is the top-4 share (63.9%)
SELECT
    srcStateName,
    ROUND(SUM(TotalFarmersCovered) / 1000000, 2) AS farmers_covered_million,
    ROUND(100 * SUM(SUM(TotalFarmersCovered)) OVER (ORDER BY SUM(TotalFarmersCovered) DESC ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING)
              / SUM(SUM(TotalFarmersCovered)) OVER (), 1) AS running_share_pct
FROM FarmersInsuranceData
GROUP BY srcStateName
ORDER BY SUM(TotalFarmersCovered) DESC
LIMIT 4;

-- Largest sums insured: Madhya Pradesh (84,132 crore, a quarter of the total) and Rajasthan (53,635 crore)
SELECT
    srcStateName,
    ROUND(SUM(SumInsured) / 100) AS sum_insured_crore,
    ROUND(100 * SUM(SumInsured) / SUM(SUM(SumInsured)) OVER (), 1) AS share_of_total_pct
FROM FarmersInsuranceData
GROUP BY srcStateName
ORDER BY SUM(SumInsured) DESC
LIMIT 2;

-- Premium split: gross 43,007 crore; farmers 5,624 (13.1%), states 19,740 (45.9%), centre 17,643 crore (41.0%)
SELECT
    ROUND(SUM(GrossPremiumAmountToBePaid) / 100) AS gross_premium_crore,
    ROUND(SUM(FarmersPremiumAmount) / 100)       AS farmers_crore,
    ROUND(SUM(StatePremiumAmount) / 100)         AS states_crore,
    ROUND(SUM(GOVPremiumAmount) / 100)           AS centre_crore,
    ROUND(100 * SUM(FarmersPremiumAmount) / SUM(GrossPremiumAmountToBePaid), 1) AS farmers_pct,
    ROUND(100 * SUM(StatePremiumAmount)   / SUM(GrossPremiumAmountToBePaid), 1) AS states_pct,
    ROUND(100 * SUM(GOVPremiumAmount)     / SUM(GrossPremiumAmountToBePaid), 1) AS centre_pct
FROM FarmersInsuranceData;

-- Per year: rows (525, 505, 429, 411), states reporting (24 to 20), farmers covered (15.0 to 10.8 million),
-- gross premium (7,263 to 13,119 crore), farmers' share of premium (19.1% to 10.6%), coverage of population (1.41% to 1.63%)
SELECT
    srcYear,
    COUNT(*)                                       AS district_rows,
    COUNT(DISTINCT srcStateName)                   AS states_reporting,
    ROUND(SUM(TotalFarmersCovered) / 1000000, 1)   AS farmers_covered_million,
    ROUND(SUM(GrossPremiumAmountToBePaid) / 100)   AS gross_premium_crore,
    ROUND(100 * SUM(FarmersPremiumAmount) / SUM(GrossPremiumAmountToBePaid), 1) AS farmers_share_pct,
    ROUND(100 * SUM(TotalFarmersCovered) / SUM(TotalPopulation), 2)             AS coverage_pct_of_population
FROM FarmersInsuranceData
GROUP BY srcYear
ORDER BY srcYear;

-- States that report only some years (Andhra Pradesh, Gujarat, Jharkhand and Telangana 2018 and 2019; West Bengal 2018)
SELECT
    srcStateName,
    GROUP_CONCAT(DISTINCT srcYear ORDER BY srcYear) AS years_reported
FROM FarmersInsuranceData
GROUP BY srcStateName
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT srcYear) < 4
ORDER BY srcStateName;

-- Highest state-years for farmers covered as a share of population (Chhattisgarh 2021 4.97%, Tripura 2020 4.68%)
SELECT
    srcStateName,
    srcYear,
    ROUND(100 * SUM(TotalFarmersCovered) / SUM(TotalPopulation), 2) AS coverage_pct_of_population
FROM FarmersInsuranceData
GROUP BY srcStateName, srcYear
ORDER BY SUM(TotalFarmersCovered) / SUM(TotalPopulation) DESC
LIMIT 2;

-- Districts with the most farmers covered (Bid first, 1.43 million)
SELECT
    srcStateName,
    srcDistrictName,
    ROUND(SUM(TotalFarmersCovered) / 1000000, 2) AS farmers_covered_million
FROM FarmersInsuranceData
GROUP BY srcStateName, srcDistrictName
ORDER BY SUM(TotalFarmersCovered) DESC
LIMIT 3;

-- The record with the highest single-year farmers' premium (Bid, 2019, 72.4 crore) also has the largest sum insured
SELECT
    srcStateName,
    srcDistrictName,
    srcYear,
    ROUND(FarmersPremiumAmount / 100, 1) AS farmers_premium_crore,
    SumInsured = (SELECT MAX(SumInsured) FROM FarmersInsuranceData) AS has_largest_sum_insured
FROM FarmersInsuranceData
WHERE FarmersPremiumAmount = (SELECT MAX(FarmersPremiumAmount) FROM FarmersInsuranceData);

-- Districts where farmers paid more than 100 crore (10,000 lakh) in total: Bid, Ujjain and Latur
SELECT
    srcStateName,
    srcDistrictName,
    ROUND(SUM(FarmersPremiumAmount) / 100, 1) AS farmers_premium_crore
FROM FarmersInsuranceData
GROUP BY srcStateName, srcDistrictName
HAVING SUM(FarmersPremiumAmount) > 10000
ORDER BY SUM(FarmersPremiumAmount) DESC;

-- Karnataka: 736,375 farmers covered against a total sum insured of 3.18 lakh
SELECT
    SUM(TotalFarmersCovered)  AS farmers_covered,
    ROUND(SUM(SumInsured), 2) AS sum_insured_lakh
```
